### Chapter 6: Expected Returns {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: sol-06-setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
library(knitr)

R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
Re <- R - rf
stopifnot(ncol(Re) == 16L, !anyNA(Re))
N <- ncol(Re); T <- nrow(Re); years <- T / 12
mu_s <- colMeans(Re); S <- stats::cov(Re)
se <- apply(Re, 2, stats::sd) * sqrt(12) / sqrt(years)

bayes_stein <- function(R, target = c("gmv", "grand")) {
  target <- match.arg(target)
  X <- zoo::coredata(R); T <- nrow(X); N <- ncol(X)
  mu   <- colMeans(X)
  S    <- stats::cov(X) * (T - 1) / (T - N - 2)
  Sinv <- solve(S); iota <- rep(1, N)
  mu0  <- if (target == "gmv") {
    as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Sinv %*% mu) / as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Sinv %*% iota)
  } else mean(mu)
  d    <- mu - mu0
  v    <- (N + 2) / ((N + 2) + T * as.numeric(t(d) %*% Sinv %*% d))
  list(mu = setNames((1 - v) * mu + v * mu0, colnames(X)), mu0 = mu0, v = v)
}

tangency_lo <- function(mu, S) {
  if (max(mu) <= 0) return(setNames(rep(NA_real_, length(mu)), names(mu)))
  N <- length(mu)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S, dvec = rep(0, N),
                            Amat = cbind(mu, diag(N)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, N)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), names(mu))
}
turnover <- function(w1, w2) sum(abs(w1[names(w2)] - w2)) / 2

# Market weights as in the chapter
eq_ids     <- sim_assets$asset_id[sim_assets$asset_class == "equity"]
region_of  <- setNames(sim_assets$region, sim_assets$asset_id)
eq_classes <- grep("_equity$", colnames(Re), value = TRUE)
cap_region <- sim_marketcap_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(asset %in% eq_ids) |>
  dplyr::mutate(class = paste0(region_of[asset], "_equity")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(date, class) |>
  dplyr::summarise(cap = sum(market_cap), .groups = "drop") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = class, values_from = cap) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
cap_mat <- as.matrix(cap_region[, eq_classes])
d <- zoo::index(Re)
W_eq <- t(vapply(seq_along(d), function(i) {
  cutoff <- if (i == 1) d[1] - 31 else d[i - 1]
  j <- max(which(cap_region$date <= cutoff))
  cap_mat[j, ] / sum(cap_mat[j, ])
}, numeric(length(eq_classes))))
colnames(W_eq) <- eq_classes
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(W_eq) - 1) < 1e-10))

proxy_weights <- function(block) {
  stopifnot(abs(sum(block) - 1) < 1e-12)
  W16 <- matrix(0, nrow(Re), N, dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(Re)))
  for (r in sub("_equity$", "", eq_classes)) {
    s <- W_eq[, paste0(r, "_equity")]
    W16[, paste0(r, "_equity")]     <- block[["equity"]]     * s
    W16[, paste0(r, "_government")] <- block[["government"]] * s
    W16[, paste0(r, "_credit")]     <- block[["credit"]]     * s
  }
  W16[, "GLOBAL_commodity"] <- block[["commodity"]]
  stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(W16) - 1) < 1e-10))
  W16
}
equilibrium <- function(W16) {
  mk <- rowSums(W16 * zoo::coredata(Re))
  delta <- mean(mk) / stats::var(mk)
  w <- colMeans(W16)
  list(mu = setNames(delta * as.numeric(S %*% w), colnames(Re)), w = w, delta = delta)
}
W16_book <- proxy_weights(c(equity = 0.40, government = 0.40, credit = 0.15, commodity = 0.05))
eq_book  <- equilibrium(W16_book)
```

#### Exercise 1

It does. @eq-06-bs-direction holds for any common target:
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\mu_0\boldsymbol{\iota}$ is the minimum-variance
direction whatever positive number $\mu_0$ is, and the target decides only how
much of it is mixed in, $v\mu_0$ against $1-v$ of the sample tangency
direction.

```{r}
#| label: sol-06-ex1
bs_gmv   <- bayes_stein(Re, "gmv")
bs_grand <- bayes_stein(Re, "grand")
w <- cbind(sample = tangency_lo(mu_s, S),
           gmv_target = tangency_lo(bs_gmv$mu, S),
           grand_target = tangency_lo(bs_grand$mu, S),
           min_variance = tangency_lo(setNames(rep(1, N), colnames(Re)), S))  # equal means
to_mv <- apply(w, 2, function(x) turnover(x, w[, "min_variance"]))  # distance to minimum variance
mix   <- function(b) b$v * b$mu0 / (1 - b$v)                        # weight on that direction
stopifnot(bs_gmv$v > bs_grand$v, mix(bs_grand) > mix(bs_gmv),
          to_mv[["gmv_target"]] < to_mv[["sample"]],
          to_mv[["grand_target"]] < to_mv[["sample"]])
c(v_gmv = bs_gmv$v, v_grand = bs_grand$v,
  mu0_gmv = bs_gmv$mu0 * 12, mu0_grand = bs_grand$mu0 * 12)
round(rbind(w[rowSums(w > 0.005) > 0, ], to_min_variance = to_mv), 3)
```

The grand mean of the sample means is
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * bs_grand$mu0 * 12)` a year against
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * bs_gmv$mu0 * 12)` for the minimum-variance target,
and $v$ is `r sprintf("%.2f", bs_grand$v)` against
`r sprintf("%.2f", bs_gmv$v)`; the higher target offsets the lower intensity
in $v\mu_0$, and the two portfolios are nearly the same. The
`US_government` weight goes from
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * w["US_government", "sample"])` in the sample
tangency to `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * w["US_government", "gmv_target"])`
with the minimum-variance target and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * w["US_government", "grand_target"])` with the grand
mean, and the turnover needed to reach the minimum-variance portfolio falls
from `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * to_mv[["sample"]])` to
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * to_mv[["gmv_target"]])` and
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * to_mv[["grand_target"]])`. The targets differ in
their argument, not in their direction: the minimum-variance return is the one
number about $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ that $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ pins down, and
the grand mean is a number with no portfolio behind it.

#### Exercise 2

```{r}
#| label: sol-06-ex2
S5 <- S[eq_classes, eq_classes]
mkt_e <- rowSums(W_eq * zoo::coredata(Re[, eq_classes]))
delta <- mean(mkt_e) / stats::var(mkt_e)
mu_avg  <- delta * as.numeric(S5 %*% colMeans(W_eq))
mu_last <- delta * as.numeric(S5 %*% W_eq[nrow(W_eq), ])
shift_se <- setNames((mu_last - mu_avg) * 12 / se[eq_classes], eq_classes)
others   <- setdiff(eq_classes, "US_equity")
stopifnot(max(abs(shift_se)) < 0.25, shift_se[["US_equity"]] > 0, all(shift_se[others] < 0),
          all(W_eq[nrow(W_eq), others] < colMeans(W_eq)[others]))
tibble::tibble(asset = eq_classes,
               average_weights = mu_avg * 12, last_weights = mu_last * 12,
               shift_in_se = shift_se) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(average_weights, last_weights), ~ sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * .x)),
                shift_in_se = sprintf("%+.2f", shift_in_se)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```

Every revision is a small fraction of a standard error, and the largest is
that of `r names(which.max(abs(shift_se)))` at
`r sprintf("%+.2f", shift_se[[which.max(abs(shift_se))]])`. The United States
gains, because its weight rises from
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * colMeans(W_eq)[["US_equity"]])` on average to
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * W_eq[nrow(W_eq), "US_equity"])` at the end of the
sample and @eq-06-equilibrium rewards whatever the market holds more of; the
four other regions lose weight and lose for the mirror-image reason,
`r names(which.min(shift_se))` most. Reverse optimization moves with the
composition of the market, which is exactly what it is supposed to do, and it
moves by far less than the sampling error of the alternative.

#### Exercise 3

```{r}
#| label: sol-06-ex3
W16_alt <- proxy_weights(c(equity = 0.60, government = 0.25, credit = 0.10, commodity = 0.05))
eq_alt  <- equilibrium(W16_alt)
shift <- (eq_alt$mu - eq_book$mu) * 12
proxy_vol <- function(W16) stats::sd(rowSums(W16 * zoo::coredata(Re))) * sqrt(12)
rest <- setdiff(names(shift), eq_classes)
stopifnot(all(shift[eq_classes] > 0), all(shift[rest] < 0), eq_alt$delta < eq_book$delta,
          proxy_vol(W16_alt) > proxy_vol(W16_book),
          isTRUE(all.equal(tangency_lo(eq_alt$mu, S), eq_alt$w, tolerance = 1e-6)))
round(sort(shift, decreasing = TRUE)[c(1:3, 14:16)] * 100, 2)
c(delta_book = eq_book$delta, delta_alt = eq_alt$delta,
  vol_book = proxy_vol(W16_book), vol_alt = proxy_vol(W16_alt))
```

Two effects meet. The equity-heavy proxy is more volatile,
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * proxy_vol(W16_alt))` a year against
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * proxy_vol(W16_book))`, so by @eq-06-delta $\delta$
falls from `r sprintf("%.1f", eq_book$delta)` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", eq_alt$delta)` and scales every element down by
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - eq_alt$delta / eq_book$delta))`, while the
heavier equity weight raises the market covariance of whatever moves with
equities. Only the five equity series end higher, by
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * min(shift[eq_classes]))` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * max(shift[eq_classes]))` percentage points; the
other `r length(rest)` fall by `r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * max(shift[rest]))` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * min(shift[rest]))`, `r names(which.min(shift))`
most. The tangency portfolio equals the new proxy weights exactly, as it must
by @eq-06-equilibrium, and that is the lesson: reverse optimization guarantees
a portfolio someone holds, and says nothing about whether the weights it was
handed are the right ones. It can be trusted to be consistent, not to be
correct.

#### Exercise 4

```{r}
#| label: sol-06-ex4
roll_turnover <- function(win) {
  starts <- seq_len(T - win + 1L)
  ws <- lapply(starts, function(s) {
    idx <- s:(s + win - 1L); X <- Re[idx, ]; Sw <- stats::cov(zoo::coredata(X))
    cbind(sample = tangency_lo(colMeans(X), Sw),
          `Bayes-Stein` = tangency_lo(bayes_stein(X)$mu, Sw),
          equilibrium = tangency_lo(eq_book$delta * as.numeric(Sw %*% colMeans(W16_book[idx, ])) |>
                                      setNames(colnames(Re)), Sw))
  })
  sapply(colnames(ws[[1]]), function(e)
    mean(vapply(2:length(ws), function(j) turnover(ws[[j - 1]][, e], ws[[j]][, e]), numeric(1))))
}
to <- rbind(`60 months` = roll_turnover(60L), `120 months` = roll_turnover(120L))
stopifnot(identical(colnames(to), c("sample", "Bayes-Stein", "equilibrium")),
          all(diff(to["60 months", ]) < 0), all(diff(to["120 months", ]) < 0))
# A rolling mean changes by (r_in - r_out) / W from one window to the next.
X <- zoo::coredata(Re)
mean_step  <- function(W) mean(abs(X[-seq_len(W), ] - X[seq_len(T - W), ])) / W
to_ratio   <- to["60 months", ] / to["120 months", ]
step_ratio <- mean_step(60L) / mean_step(120L)
stopifnot(to_ratio[["sample"]] > sqrt(2), abs(step_ratio - 2) < 0.1)
round(to, 4)
round(c(to_ratio, mean_step = step_ratio), 2)
```

The ranking is unchanged: the sample mean moves most, Bayes-Stein less, the
equilibrium hardly at all. Doubling the window cuts the sample-mean turnover
by a factor of `r sprintf("%.2f", to_ratio[["sample"]])`, not by the
$\sqrt{2}$ that @eq-06-se predicts for the standard error of the mean.
@eq-06-se compares independent samples, and consecutive windows share
`r 120L - 1L` of `r 120L` months: the mean changes by
$(r_{\text{in}} - r_{\text{out}})/W$ from one window to the next, a step that
falls by a factor of `r sprintf("%.2f", step_ratio)` when $W$ doubles, and
the turnover follows it.
